sentences.text_en: Every afternoon, An and Jo crossed a narrow wooden bridge on their way to the reading club.
One day, An heard a small scratching sound beneath the first plank.
Jo was already halfway across, talking loudly about a story with a flying bicycle.
An raised a hand and asked her to stop for a moment.
Through a gap, he could see a nest with two young birds near the bank.
The parent bird waited on a branch with a seed in its beak.
Each time someone stamped across the bridge, it flew farther away instead of approaching the nest.
An did not try to touch the birds or move their nest.
He suggested that they take the longer stone path beside the pond for a few days.
Jo looked at her watch because the reading club would begin soon.
“We can walk quickly on the path without making the bridge shake,” she said.
They arrived at the club a little later than usual and explained the reason.
On the next afternoon, they saw the parent bird reach the nest while the bridge was quiet.
They kept their distance and watched for only a minute before taking the stone path again.

lessons.title_en: Two Ways to Share the Shade

source.attribution: Original Read2Lead project draft, Codex for Coach Felix, 2026-09-18

objectives: Compare responses, interpret changing feelings and contextual vocabulary with evidence.

sentences.text_en: The school gardening group had one large cloth to shade its young plants during a week of strong sunshine.
Nora suggested stretching the cloth over the vegetable bed, where several leaves had begun to curl at the edges.
Duc preferred putting it over the new flower pots because the younger class had planted them only yesterday.
At first, Nora thought Duc cared more about attractive flowers than the vegetables everyone had worked on for a month.
She folded her arms and pointed at a drooping bean plant.
Instead of arguing, Duc showed her a note from the younger class: their pots were too heavy for the children to carry inside.
Nora unfolded her arms and asked whether the pots could be moved on the group’s small trolley.
Together they tested the trolley with one pot, holding it steady as they crossed the uneven path.
The test worked, although moving every pot would take longer than simply covering them.
They agreed to wheel the pots under the veranda and keep the cloth above the vegetable bed.
Two classmates offered to help with the trolley, so the younger children only needed to guide them to the right pots.
By lunchtime, both areas had shade, but Nora and Duc were tired and had not finished labelling the seedlings.
“Our plan costs more time,” Nora said, “but now neither group loses the shade it needs.”
Duc nodded and suggested finishing the labels during the next gardening session.
Nora wrote down the route that had worked, including the uneven corner, so another group could move the pots safely later.

Nora suggested stretching the cloth over the vegetable bed, where several leaves had begun to curl at the edges. Duc preferred putting it over the new flower pots because the younger class had planted them only yesterday. At first, Nora thought Duc cared more about attractive flowers than the vegetables everyone had worked on for a month. She folded her arms and pointed at a drooping bean plant. Instead of arguing, Duc showed her a note from the younger class: their pots were too heavy for the children to carry inside. Nora unfolded her arms and asked whether the pots could be moved on the group’s small trolley. Together they tested the trolley with one pot, holding it steady as they crossed the uneven path. The test worked, although moving every pot would take longer than simply covering them. They agreed to wheel the pots under the veranda and keep the cloth above the vegetable bed. Two classmates offered to help with the trolley, so the younger children only needed to guide them to the right pots. By lunchtime, both areas had shade, but Nora and Duc were tired and had not finished labelling the seedlings. “Our plan costs more time,” Nora said, “but now neither group loses the shade it needs.” Duc nodded and suggested finishing the labels during the next gardening session. Nora wrote down the route that had worked, including the uneven corner, so another group could move the pots safely later.

sentences.text_en: A student council was deciding whether a small rain tank should supply the school garden throughout the next dry month.
The proposal sounded simple: collect roof water after rain, then use it instead of tap water whenever the beds needed watering.
Amir’s group measured the tank for one week and reported that it held enough water for four ordinary watering days.
During that week, however, rain fell on three afternoons and the vegetable beds were partly shaded.
Their report concluded, “The tank can provide all the water our garden needs.”
A second group kept an older gardening diary covering a hot week without rain.
The diary said that the beds needed almost twice as much water as usual, and one leaking hose had wasted an unknown amount.
The diary did not record the exact size of the planted area, which had since increased.
At the council meeting, some students argued that the recent measurements were more useful because they described the current garden.
Others thought the older diary proved that a rain tank could never be useful.
Lea disagreed with both absolute conclusions: each source described conditions that were different from the proposed dry month.
She suggested using the tank as a supplementary supply while measuring daily demand, rainfall and losses with the leak repaired.
Amir worried that keeping tap water available would make students forget to collect rainwater at all.
Lea proposed a clear routine: check the tank first, record how much is used, and take additional water only when the plants need it.
The council accepted a limited trial instead of promising that the tank would replace the tap completely.
They would compare records after two weeks, including days when the tank was empty, before deciding whether to change its size.
No one could yet say how much money the plan would save, because the price of a larger tank and the cost of maintenance had not been collected.
Amir revised the final heading to “What our tank supplied this week, and what we still need to find out.”

audio.script_en: A student council was deciding whether a small rain tank should supply the school garden throughout the next dry month. The proposal sounded simple: collect roof water after rain, then use it instead of tap water whenever the beds needed watering. Amir’s group measured the tank for one week and reported that it held enough water for four ordinary watering days. During that week, however, rain fell on three afternoons and the vegetable beds were partly shaded. Their report concluded, “The tank can provide all the water our garden needs.” A second group kept an older gardening diary covering a hot week without rain. The diary said that the beds needed almost twice as much water as usual, and one leaking hose had wasted an unknown amount. The diary did not record the exact size of the planted area, which had since increased. At the council meeting, some students argued that the recent measurements were more useful because they described the current garden. Others thought the older diary proved that a rain tank could never be useful. Lea disagreed with both absolute conclusions: each source described conditions that were different from the proposed dry month. She suggested using the tank as a supplementary supply while measuring daily demand, rainfall and losses with the leak repaired. Amir worried that keeping tap water available would make students forget to collect rainwater at all. Lea proposed a clear routine: check the tank first, record how much is used, and take additional water only when the plants need it. The council accepted a limited trial instead of promising that the tank would replace the tap completely. They would compare records after two weeks, including days when the tank was empty, before deciding whether to change its size. No one could yet say how much money the plan would save, because the price of a larger tank and the cost of maintenance had not been collected. Amir revised the final heading to “What our tank supplied this week, and what we still need to find out.”

options_en: The tank will always supply the whole garden.

accepted_meanings: It supplied useful water in one week, but neither report establishes full dry-month coverage.

evidence_spans.quote: Amir’s group measured the tank for one week and reported that it held enough water for four ordinary watering days.
